title: Chapter 173 – The Wall Shakes
html:
[The Lin Garden – Feng]

Feng has not slept a full night in twenty-nine years, and tonight the earth will not let him pretend.

He lies on the narrow cot in the ridge-house with his hands folded on his chest and his eyes open, and he listens. It is what he does. It is what he has done since the night, long ago, when the silver thread was drawn through his marrow and the Purple Mansion opened behind his eyes. The world is not quiet. It has never been quiet again. Under every floor and every road and every hill, there are seams: the long thin cracks where one thing meets another, where stone meets stone and water meets root and the living meets the dead. And all of them hum.

Most nights it is a low steady drone, like a hive heard through a wall. He has learned to rest within it. He lies on the cot and lets the hum wash over him, and sometimes, near dawn, a gray thin sleep comes and takes an hour.

Tonight the hum has teeth.

It began at the third watch. A flutter, at first, from the north, so faint that he thought it was the pulse in his own ears. Then a long falling note, as of a great bell struck far underground. Then another. Now, two hours before dawn, the whole hillside is shaking with a sound that he feels not in his ears but in his teeth, in his knuckles, in the soles of his feet. It is a hundred thousand voices, all singing the same low furious word.

He sits up. He puts both feet on the floor. The boards are trembling.

Hu's red-wood staff leans against the wall, where it has leaned for nearly thirty years. It is dark with handling, and the grain is polished like glass. He takes it in both hands and plants the butt on the floor, and the hum thins, a little, as it always does when the damping grain drinks the worst of it. It is not a cure. It is a hand over an ear.

"Right," he says to the empty room. His voice is rough. "That's enough of that."

He puts on his boots.

* * *

The horn comes just before dawn.

It is a long, cracked, ragged blast, from the north, from the Wall. He has heard it five times in his life, and each time it was a drill. This is not a drill. The note falls and rises and does not stop, and behind it, thin and high, a second horn answers, and a third.

By the time Feng reaches the Garden Hall the courtyard is full.

They are all there, or nearly all: the guards in their quilted tunics, the elders in their winter gowns, the clerks with their lamps and ledgers and their sleeves rolled to the elbow. A cold gray light is breaking over the roof-tiles. Someone has lit the great brazier at the center of the yard, and the shadows leap. Voices shout from every side. A dog is howling. At the foot of the Hall steps, small and square in a plain brown robe, with a rod of black iron in her hand, stands Zhao.

She is the head of the clan, now. She has been so for a good many years. She is past eighty, and does not look it, and when Feng comes through the crowd she looks up with a small grim smile.

"You're late," she says.

"I was listening."

"I know." She lowers her voice. "What does it sound like?"

He does not answer at once. He stands beside her on the step, with Hu's staff planted in front of him, and looks over the heads of the crowd at the pale sky. The hum is in the stones beneath his feet. It is in the brazier's iron legs. It is in the very air.

"Like a lot of people knocking," he says slowly. "On a door."

Zhao's mouth tightens. She nods. She turns to the courtyard and raises the rod, and the noise falls away.

"Clan of the Garden," she says. "The Wall has called us."

* * *

The messenger is a boy of seventeen, and he is shaking.

He has ridden all night, from the Sect lines. His horse is lathered white. He sits on the step of the Hall with a bowl of hot tea in both hands, and Pei An, thin and gray and precise, with a clerk's ink-stained cuffs, stands over him with a lamp and a writing board, taking down what he says in short fast strokes.

"It began at midnight," the boy says. "The pickets heard it first. A sound like thunder, but from the ground. Then the dogs went mad. Then the first of them came over the ridge."

"What came?" asks Zhao.

"Crawlers, madam. And Gnashers. A few Riders." He swallows. "Head Han says four thousand, perhaps more. The lines are holding. The lines will hold. But he says to tell you—" He stops. His eyes are huge. "He says the Pass is full, madam. All the way to the Seven Winds. He says there's no end to them."

A murmur runs through the courtyard.

Pei An looks up from his board. "And Head Han's request?"

"Two hundred guards, madam. And the Garden's stores. And—" the boy hesitates "—he says to tell Elder Feng that he is to come himself. If he is willing. He says the Wall needs someone who can hear."

Every head turns.

Feng looks at the boy. Then he looks at the sky, and the Hall roof, and the long gray line of the northern hills. The hum rises in his ears. He closes his hand on the staff.

"I'll come," he says.

"Feng," says Zhao, quietly.

"I'll come. But I want to say something first." He faces the courtyard. His voice is dry and flat, as it always is, but the crowd goes still. "I've been listening since the third watch. I want everyone to hear what I think."

He draws a breath.

"They are not only at the Wall."

* * *

It takes him a quarter of an hour to say it, and he hates every minute.

He stands on the steps of the Garden Hall with the red staff in his hand and tries, in his awkward careful voice, to describe something that has no words. The hum is not in one place. It has layers. There is a loud sharp rhythm to the north, the hard clamor of beasts on the surface, beating at the Sect lines like surf. But under it, deeper, there is another note. A slow wide grinding sound that does not come from the north at all.

It comes from below.

"They're digging," he says. "I think. Or something is. It's deep. Fifty fathoms, maybe more. I can feel it in the bedrock. It's going the other way."

"Which way?" asks Pei An, sharply.

"South. Toward us."

Silence.

"There is a Wall," says Zhao slowly. "A great stone Wall. With two thousand men on it. And the beasts are going around it? Under it?"

"I don't know what they're doing." Feng's hand is tight on the staff. "I only know what I hear. And what I hear is that the Wall is the loud part. The thing under it is the quiet part. And I've been in enough fights to know which of the two to be afraid of."

The courtyard stirs. Someone mutters. A guard at the back says, loudly, "He's an old man. He's been sleepless for thirty years. He's hearing ghosts."

Feng turns his head. The guard flushes and subsides.

"I could be wrong," Feng says evenly. "I've been wrong before. But I'd rather be wrong in a shelter than right in a ditch."

Zhao looks at him for a long moment. Then she lifts her chin.

"Pei An," she says. "How long does it take to move the Garden's stores to the Hall cellars?"

"A day."

"Do it in six hours." She turns. "Lan Wen. The two hundred. Take them north, as Head Han requests. And take every man who can hold a spear."

"And Feng?" Lan Wen's pale eyes are steady, white as river ice. "He's wanted at the Wall."

"He is." Zhao faces him. "But if he's right—"

"Then someone must listen here," says Feng.

* * *

Lan Wen rides out at mid-morning, and Feng walks him to the gate.

The captain of the guard is a tall man, narrow-faced, with hair like frost and eyes so pale they seem to have no color at all. He wears a plain steel breastplate over a gray tunic, and a long spear rides in a socket at his saddle. Behind him the column forms, two hundred men in good order, with their cloaks rolled and their jaws set. A banner snaps from a pole: the Garden's mark, a green pine on white.

"You'll hold the Hall," says Lan Wen.

"I'll try."

"If I'm wrong, and the beasts are only at the Wall, you'll have lost a morning for nothing."

"If you're wrong, I'll buy you a drink."

The white eyes gleam. "I will hold you to it." He gathers the reins. Then, as the column begins to move, he leans down from the saddle, and says in a voice so low that only Feng can hear it: "I did not know my name for a long time. You know that."

"I know."

"Do you know what it was like, when I got it back?" He doesn't wait. "It was like being let in out of the cold. I would like to be worth the name, before the end."

"You are."

"Thank you." A small stiff smile. "Look after Pei An. He pretends to be unafraid. He is not."

"I know."

"Good." Lan Wen straightens. "Garden!" he shouts. "Forward!"

The column moves out through the gate. Feng stands watching it go, the green banner dwindling down the northern road, and a strange cold weight settles in his chest.

He has been listening a long time. He thinks, for a moment, that he knows what he is hearing.

* * *

He stops at the kitchen first, because he always does.

It is the biggest room in the Garden, a long low hall of whitewashed brick with a dozen hearths along one wall and a ceiling blackened by a century of smoke. At this hour it is already roaring. Cooks in floured aprons hurry between the tables with trays of steaming rice cakes. Boys with buckets of water run in and out. And at the far end, by the largest hearth, stirring a cauldron the size of a bath with a paddle as long as a spear, stands Qinghe.

She is old. She is also, by the look of her, perhaps fifty. Her face is lined, and strong, and brown from the fire; her hair is pinned under a white cloth; her sleeves are rolled to the elbow over forearms like a refiner's. She does not look round when he comes in. She holds out a hand, without turning, and a cook slaps a bowl into it, and she dips and holds it out behind her.

"Eat," she says.

He takes it. It is rice porridge, thick with ginger and spring onion. He doesn't need her to tell him that she cannot taste it. He has known for thirty-seven years that she cannot taste anything. And he knows, from the sheer unerring perfection of the seasoning, that she doesn't need to.

"You've heard," he says.

"The whole Garden has heard." She tastes nothing, and nods at the ladle, and a boy takes it away. "Is it bad?"

"It's loud."

"That's not what I asked."

He eats a mouthful of porridge. It is exactly right. He swallows, and says, "It's bad."

Qinghe nods. She puts down the paddle. For a moment her hands rest on the rim of the cauldron, large and scarred and still. "Then I'll want the cellars aired," she says. "And every pot we own scrubbed and filled. If this lasts as long as you think, they'll need to eat."

"Qinghe—"

"Don't tell me not to. I've been feeding this clan since before you could walk. I'm not stopping now." She wipes her hands on her apron. Her eyes, when they find his, are black and bright and entirely unafraid. "When you hear him coming, tell me. I'd like to have the kettle on."

He stares at her. "Who?"

"You know who." And the corner of her mouth lifts. "Little stone."

* * *

Wenyuan does not wake.

Feng stands at the foot of the great carved bed in the east room, with his staff in his hand and the gray morning light on the bedclothes, and looks at the old man. He is past a hundred and ten. His beard is white and spread over the blanket like frost. His hands lie folded on his breast, thin and cold and spotted. He breathes. It is the slow, deep, unhurried breath of the winter sleep, the breath of a bear in a cave, and it will not change until the thaw.

It is not winter yet. It is the very end of autumn. But the sleep has been coming sooner every year, and tonight, Feng thinks, it came in the middle of the afternoon.

"Father," he says.

No answer.

"Father. It's me. Feng." He lays a hand on the thin shoulder. "The tide's come. The Wall's under attack. I thought you should know."

The old man's lips move.

It is such a small movement that Feng nearly misses it. A trembling of the dry mouth, a faint shape, and then, in a voice like paper rubbed on paper, a single word.

"Stone."

"What?"

"Little stone." The eyes do not open. A frail smile creeps across the lined face. "Coming home."

Feng's throat tightens. He kneels by the bed, and takes the cold hand in both of his, and holds it for a long time, listening to the old man breathe. Outside, the horn is calling. Beneath him, the floor is trembling. But in the east room there is a stillness, and a smell of old paper and camphor, and an old man's smile.

"I'll tell him," he says. "I'll tell him you said."

* * *

At noon he goes to the tree.

He has not meant to. He is walking down the hill from the tower with the staff in his hand, thinking of nothing, and his feet take him through the apple rows and out to the low rise where the great black trunk stands. It is the oldest thing in the Garden. Qinghe planted it as a sapling, in the year Jian was born. It is now taller than the Hall, and thicker through than three men can reach round, and its bark is black and ridged like the back of some ancient beast. Its leaves are silver. In the noon light they move, though there is no wind.

He lays his palm on the trunk.

It is warm. It has always been warm. And under his hand, as he has known for years, it hums. A low steady note, slow, deep, patient, a note he has never been able to place in any of the seams he hears. It is not stone. It is not water. It is something he has no word for.

Today there is something more.

He shuts his eyes. He lets the hum rise through his arm, into his skull, and he listens. Beneath the note, faint and thin, in the way of a thing heard from a very great distance, he hears a voice.

It is singing.

It is a woman's voice. Or a girl's. Or perhaps neither: a high, quiet, wordless tune, with a lilt in it, as of a lullaby sung in an empty room. It is not meant for him. It is not meant for anyone. It is simply there, in the wood, the way a smell is in a loaf of bread.

He stands for a long time with his hand on the bark and his eyes shut.

When he opens them, the leaves are very still. And the sun has gone behind a cloud.

* * *

He goes up to the tower on the ridge, at midday, with Ning Ruiyan.

It is a stone watch-tower, three stories high, built by the clan's carpenters in the first year of Ning's residence. She keeps her instruments in the upper room: brass rings, a great bronze disc, a bank of slender lenses on a pivot. She has charted the sky above the Garden for twenty-five years. She is broad and scarred and ink-stained, with a sharp eye, and she does not look up when Feng comes through the door.

"Don't talk," she says. "I'm busy."

"The ring—"

"The ring is lit." She does not turn. "It's been lit since midnight. In daylight."

He crosses the room and stands behind her. On the great bronze disc, which is set into the floor and marked with fifty-four notches, there is a thin bright circle of white fire. It burns steadily. It does not flicker. In the brass lenses overhead, if he looks, he can see a smear of silver across the blue noon.

"What does it mean?" he asks.

"It means the eleven stars have lit." Ning's voice is low. "All of them. At once. In the day. I've never seen it. The chart says they only ever darken." She straightens. "Feng. I have been watching that ring since the year I was named. I have watched it dim, on every winter solstice, for twenty-five years. Whatever it is, it was never meant to light."

"A warning?"

"A bell." She finally turns, and her eyes are bright and fierce. "Someone is ringing it. On purpose."

He thinks of a long road. He thinks of a white-haired man and a staff, walking north. He thinks of a girl with a pebble at her throat.

"Jian," he says.

"I don't know." Ning's mouth tightens. "But the ring points north. And south. And down."

Feng stands very still. He is listening. The hum is in his bones, in the stone, in the brass. And beneath it, deep and slow and unmistakable, he hears the grinding. It is closer. He is almost certain that it is closer.

"Ning," he says. "How long before sunset?"

"Six hours."

"Then I think we have until about then."

* * *

Pei An works through the afternoon in the cellars, with a lamp on his shoulder and a ledger on his knee.

He has never learned to hold a spear. He has never wanted to. He is a thin stooping man of seventy-nine, with a stick and a cheerful face, a clerk's cuffs and a clerk's squint, and he walks the length of the Hall cellars with a quill behind his ear, counting. Three hundred sacks of rice. Eleven barrels of salt fish. Forty jars of preserved plums. A rack of lamp oil, a stack of blankets, a chest of bandages, a crate of Bell's old bone-setting splints. He ticks them off in his small neat hand and moves on.

Feng follows him down, because he cannot sit still.

"Eleven hundred souls," says Pei An, without looking up. "Seven hundred in the cellars. The rest in the Hall proper, the school, the bell tower. Two weeks of food, if no one is greedy. Three, if we ration."

"And if it lasts longer than three?"

"Then I shall have to learn to cook." The clerk's mouth quirks. "I have noticed that Qinghe does not like to be helped."

"She does not."

Pei An sets down his quill. For a moment the lamp makes a small yellow circle on the damp stone, and in it the old man's face looks suddenly very tired. "Feng," he says. "Do you know what I was, before I was this?"

"A clerk of the Second House."

"A third clerk. In a room with forty others, copying the names of the dead onto plum-bark paper in a hand that was not mine." He folds his hands. "I did it for twenty-two years. I thought it was a safe job. I thought that if I kept my head down and my ink dry, nothing would ever happen to me."

"And then?"

"And then I read a roll of a hundred and nineteen names, and I understood what I had been doing." A thin smile. "I have not kept my head down since."

Feng says nothing. The old clerk picks up his quill.

"If there are to be dead," says Pei An, "I should like to be the one who writes them. Properly. In my own hand. I do not think anyone else will have the stomach for it."

He turns back to his ledger. The lamp-flame wavers. Overhead, through six feet of stone, the hum goes on.

* * *

Kuang finds him on the stair.

He is thirteen. He has his mother's square jaw and his father's long legs, and an expression of sullen determination that Feng recognizes from every boy of that age he has ever met. He stands three steps above, with his arms folded and a wooden practice sword thrust through his belt.

"I'm going to the Wall," says Kuang.

"No."

"Lan Wen said I could come when I was fourteen."

"You're thirteen."

"In a month."

"In a month, you can argue it with your mother." Feng leans on his staff. "Right now you're going to carry water to the cellars, like everyone else who is too young to stand in a line."

The boy's jaw sets. "That's not fair."

"No."

"I can fight. I've been practicing."

"I know. I've watched you." Feng gives him a long look. "You're good. You'll be better. But you're thirteen, and there are four thousand beasts on the Wall, and I do not want to be the one to tell Zhao you went."

Kuang's shoulders sag. He scuffs the toe of one boot on the stone. After a while he says, in a smaller voice, "Do you think it'll be bad?"

Feng weighs the answer. He could lie. He is not a man who lies well.

"Yes," he says. "I think it'll be very bad. Probably the worst thing any of us has seen."

"Oh."

"But here's what I've learned." He lowers himself onto the step with a grunt, and the red staff rests across his knees. "A wall holds if there's someone behind it who's willing to carry the water. It's not glorious. Nobody writes songs about it. But it's the difference."

Kuang looks at him. "You're really not going to let me go."

"Not today."

"Fine." The boy sighs, with enormous drama. He unhooks the practice sword, and lays it carefully on the stair. Then he picks up the bucket that has been sitting at his feet all along, and starts down.

"Kuang."

"What?"

"The man you were named for laughed like someone falling over a chair." Feng says it softly. "Qinghe told me. I thought you should hear it from someone who knew him."

The boy stands very still, with his back to Feng. His shoulders are rigid. Then, without turning, he says in a thick voice, "Thanks."

"Go and carry your water."

He goes.

* * *

At dusk the orchard begins to scream.

He is standing on the Hall steps with the red staff in his hand and the courtyard emptying around him, the last of the stores being carried down into the cellars, the last of the clerks hurrying with their lamps. The sun is a red coin on the western ridge. The wind has dropped. And from the orchard, from the low hill at the foot of the Garden where the old Burned Orchard stood, a sound comes up that he has never heard before.

It is a trees' cry. Wooden. Long. Tearing.

He is running before he knows. Zhao is beside him, and Pei An, and a handful of guards. They pelt down the hill through the dusk, between the dark rows of the new apple trees, and the screaming grows. The air smells of earth, and sap, and something else, something cold and iron and wrong.

At the bottom of the orchard they stop.

The hill is heaving.

It is the only word. The ground under the oldest of the trees, the black-barked giant that Qinghe planted with her own hands, is rising and falling like the chest of a sleeping thing. The grass splits. The roots stand up out of the soil in great black arches, groaning. A crack opens, wide as a cart track, and runs across the slope, and from it steam begins to rise.

"Back!" shouts Zhao. "Everyone back!"

Nobody moves. They stand in a half circle, transfixed. Feng feels the hum in his skull rise to a howl. He sees, in the crack, a movement.

A pale shape. Wet. Many-jointed. It lifts out of the earth like a drowned man rising from a pond, and behind it comes another, and another, and the crack becomes a mouth, a black seething mouth, spilling pale legs and bone-rimmed heads onto the dusk-colored grass.

Crawlers.

Thirty. Fifty. They pour up out of the hill in a silent flood, and the first of them lifts its blind head and turns toward the Garden, and the dusk fills with the thin dry clicking of a thousand hooked legs.

Zhao lifts her iron rod. Her voice is perfectly calm.

"Ring the bell," she says.

Feng plants his staff, and listens, and hears under the clicking, under the screaming of the orchard, under the whole grinding furious dark, a single slow beat, like a heart.

It is coming up through the roots.

It is coming for the tree.
